en: Having weapons readied,
Having swift horses tethered for war,
He made our whole world complete.
Since coming to Khan Manas,
We matured and became warriors,
The equals of heroes' sons.
We strapped our quivers at our sides;
The countless troops that came to joust
We shattered, leaving not one.
Among Afghans and Qizilbash,
We made steeds rear within their courts.
Of the Russians and Jurchens,
We took the daughters captive and made them weep.
Who dwelt at Chambyl-Bel,
The two heroes Zhanaaly and Karach,
Said to be warriors of terrible strength—
Their raised standards we brought down.
We felled all who faced us.
From the massive gated fortress,
For blue-maned sovereign Bakay,
Körpayan, the surpassingly beautiful girl,
We brought as an offering from the court.
The blue-maned leopard, lord of battle,
Never turned his wrath upon us.
However much of his wealth we scattered,
He never grew displeased.
Since coming to Khan Manas,
The forty companions have no regrets.
For you to wear, hero Manas
Gave white-fibered silk and skilled craftswomen.
In crimson dresses, slender-waisted,
Thimble-mouthed, with camel-calf eyes,
With thick hair flowing playfully,
He stormed courts and gave us girls.
He shattered the Oirats and made us warriors.
When we consider it, hero Manas
Made us khans over settled peoples.
If we do not bring our horses as offerings,
If we do not receive the generous one's blessing,
We shall become infidels.”
Leopard Manas, lord of battle—
Among twelve nations' multitudes,
To mighty, blue-maned Manas
None remained to show defiance.
Going inward by the direct way,
To your generous Khan Manas,
Sarala and Kögala,
Almambet and Chubak, the two warriors,
Brought them by the lead.
They turned their heads toward the lion.
To their lion, generous Manas,
The two warriors grinned,
Offering their two horses.
“Forgive our sin!” they now pleaded.
“Almambet, Chubak, my heroes,
My matched pair of champions,
My valley full of meadowsweet,
When an enemy comes to smash us,
My tireless stalwarts!
Almambet, Chubak, my twins,
My bright and boundless sea,
When an enemy comes shooting,
My strength that could shatter the whole world!
To the splendid city of Beijing,
When setting out to reach and scout it,
You caught up and started a quarrel;
Shameless Chubak, shame upon you!
When I reached you and held you back,
You spoke one word to the full;
That word shames us, Almambet!
‘Be not merely darkness, but night,’ you said,
‘Join forces with your khan,’ you said;
You delivered it as plainly as writing.
Look at your words: shame upon you, Almambet!
Your hurtful words shame us, Almambet!
In the tamarisk-filled lowlands of Talas,
When have I scattered what I gathered,
Made my word two,
Let my good conduct fail,
When have I betrayed my faith?
‘Not merely darkness, but night,’ you said,
‘Join forces with your khan,’ you said.
What business has such talk, Almambet?!”
Hearing this, Almambet,
The blood draining from his face,
Turned sideways in anger.
At blue-maned leopard Manas
He looked and began to speak:
“Even if Chinese, a man is great;
Chubak, with a homeland, is mighty.
I, poor wretch, estranged from my homeland,
I see, am miserable and despised.
Rather than a young man live,
Rather than endure such humiliation,
It would be better for him to die!
Even if an infidel, a man is mighty;
Chubak, with a people, is great.
I, poor wretch, estranged from my people,
Rather than cast a shadow in this world,
It would be better for me to die!
A man with a people is mighty;
One estranged from his people is despised.
Whenever they think of it, they call me Chinese;
This too is Almambet's misfortune!
Even if I scout the whole world,
How many years have passed since I came?
Will my name ‘Chinese’ ever leave me?!
When I lived in Beijing,
I renounced my idol,
I shattered my own people.
When I lived in Beijing,
I was a cliff no goose could circle.
As you know, Khan Manas,
I was an impregnable dark mountain.
When I lived in Beijing,
When angry, I was night.
Of the vast Black Chinese people,
I was their emperor's son.
For him to trot along the road,
For him to pursue me from behind,
For him to call me a foolish Chinese,
As though I had plundered his cloth,
As though I had come stirring up trouble—
Think a little, O Manas!
When was I a slave to the Noygut?”
Your champion Manas, lord of battle,
Stood looking without a word.
He pondered, shaking his head,
Silent for as long as a meal takes to cook.
Then Manas thought;
This was what he thought.
The mighty one's thoughts
The two champions did not know.
“If the devil Azazil misled me,
If he suddenly led me astray,
If I took the path of darkness,
My vast Muslim people
Abandoned to desolation,
And fled to Beijing,
And settled there in a camp,
In the Chinese realm's Beijing,
If I served without stint...”
Tal-Choku was a lofty mountain;
All around were rocky cliffs,
Precipices beyond the reach of sight.
Flowing at its foot
Was a river of powerful current.
Lined along the river
Were many hills.
Soaring Tal-Choku,
With its high mountain pass,
Between Beijing and Mecca,
Between those two vast peoples,
It stood as a fortress.
The giant black bird and fanged beasts
Made their home in that place.
If one did not cross it,
To travel all around
Was a journey of forty days.
No mortal had crossed it;
The path was a lofty precipice,
Its ledge was difficult and narrow.
Above the narrow ledge
Was a black stone big as a house.
If you looked atop the stone,
A great goshawk had built its nest.
Coiling round and hissing,
A dragon had encircled it.
When they saw the dragon,
Almambet and Chubak, the two warriors,
Fell with a thud from their horses,
And lost consciousness.
Leopard Manas, the noble lion,
To the great stone where the dragon lay
Now deliberately walked.
His knees bent toward the earth;
He sprang forward and ran,
Muttering and gathering his strength,
Facing toward the west,
Manas strode with ringing steps;
The dragon fled in a flash.
Almambet and Chubak
Stirred and got to their feet.
Their eyes opened clear again;
The two lions who had lain numb
Bowed their heads toward Manas.
The pillar of the companions,
Manas was the warrior's support.
When the journey's road was long,
When there were countless hosts of troops,
Hero Manas was the people's prop.
His world was complete.
Ocean-like leopard Manas—
His heart was wider than a lake,
He was a hero born a lion.
Poison to the foes who faced him,
He was a hero who had conquered many.
Then Almambet and Chubak, the two lions, said:
“Who has crossed Tal-Choku?
Saying, ‘I shall bring affliction on Beijing,
And the teeming multitudes of Chinese
I shall conquer and subdue,’
The hero Rustam Dastan crossed it.
Who shall cross it after him?
The lion Manas shall cross!”
There was writing on the black stone.
When they read that writing,
There were the names of two men.
Cliffs surrounded it;
Apart from those two men,
No others were in that inscription.
The hero Manas, born a leopard,
Leaning upon his battle-axe,
Looking at the way ahead,
Mounted Aybanboz beneath him
And headed for Tal-Choku.
Above Tal-Choku,
The haze scattered,
And the clouds parted.
Traveling until evening,
Going far without a rest,
He reached the peak at dusk.
As he approached Tal-Choku,
There was snow upon its mountain;
In the hollow at its foot,
Tall willows grew.
Its flat top jutted out in angles.
When one came to Tal-Choku,
A fragrant scent arose.
Spring waters spread in streams.
Between Mecca and Beijing
It stood as a fortress,
Strong on every side.
Considering it, Tal-Choku
Was a place to leave the rear camp.
After they had seen that place,
And tested and learned its true nature,
Almambet, Chubak, and the hero Syrgak—
Kogala and Sarala,
Kokchebich, Kurong, and Aybanboz—
They took off the saddles, leaving the horses bare,
Tied their heads high and tethered their feet.
With their keen steel weapons at their sides,
And white saddles beneath their heads,
Lying with their heads toward the west,
The four champions who had come from afar
Sank into a mighty sleep.
Once they had fallen fast asleep,
A black-spotted leopard
Poised itself at his side;
A black-eared lion
Charged furiously at Manas.
When he saw this dream,
Manas awoke from sleep
And turned onto his right side.
The sky darkened and grew overcast;
